Leonard Busher
len'ərd boosh'ər
n. (Leonard Busher, fl. 1614, English Baptist of Amsterdam, author of Religions Peace, the earliest printed English plea for liberty of conscience)
English surname Busher, a variant of Bussher, a dweller by the bushes; Leonard, lion-strong.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Leonard Busher describes himself as a citizen of London living in Amsterdam, and almost nothing else about him is certain. What survives is the tract: Religions Peace: or A Plea for Liberty of Conscience, addressed to King James and Parliament and printed in 1614, the earliest known English publication demanding full liberty of conscience in religion. Busher argued that faith is the gift of God and cannot be commanded by statute, that the apostles converted men by preaching and not by prisons, that the forcing of conscience fills the church with hypocrites, and that heretics are to be met with the word. He proposed in plain terms that any man be allowed to write, dispute, or print on religion, provided he kept the civil peace. Isa 55:11 is the confidence the whole plea rests on, that God's word “shall not return unto me void” (Isa 55:11) and therefore needs no sword.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines liberty as freedom from restraint, and persecution as the infliction of pain or death for adherence to a particular creed.

expand to see more

LIB'ERTY, n. Freedom from restraint, in a general sense, and applicable to the body, or to the will or mind.

PERSECU'TION, n. The act or practice of persecuting; the infliction of pain, punishment or death upon others unjustly, particularly for adhering to a religious creed.

HYP'OCRITE, n. One who feigns to be what he is not; one who has the form of godliness without the power.

Key Scripture

Isa 55:11 — "So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it."

Joh 4:24 — "God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth."

1Ti 2:2 — "For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty."

Mat 20:25 — "But Jesus called them unto him, and said, Ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them, and they that are great exercise authority upon them."

Modern Corruption

A London exile printed the first English demand for full liberty of conscience and then vanished from the record.

expand to see more

Busher's central observation is one that persecuting establishments never make about themselves: compulsion does not produce faith, it produces conformity, and a church filled with conformists has been weakened rather than strengthened by the law that filled it. Joh 4:24 requires worship in spirit and in truth, and the state can secure neither. Mat 20:25 describes the exercise of dominion as the way of the princes of the Gentiles, and Mat 20:26 says it shall not be so among Christ's servants.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the confidence underneath the plea. Busher was not an indifferentist; he held the gospel to be true and believed that truth does not require protection by penalty, because Isa 55:11 promises that the word accomplishes what God pleases. The modern mistake runs the other way: liberty of conscience is now commonly argued from the premise that religious claims are not the kind of thing that can be true. Busher argued it from the premise that his were, and that is the only form of the argument a church can honestly make.

Usage

"“it shall not return unto me void” (Isa 55:11) — why the word needs no sword."

"“they that are great exercise authority upon them” (Mat 20:25) — the Gentile way."

"“in all godliness and honesty” (1Ti 2:2) — what is asked of rulers."
